# readme-writer — Full AI Reference

> Self-contained reference for AI agents and LLM-based search systems. `readme-writer` is an Agent Skill (Python, MIT, v0.2.0) by Tatsuya Shimomoto (@shimo4228) that writes and repairs human-facing READMEs. It is the human-surface counterpart to llms-txt-writer.

## Project Facts

- **Name**: readme-writer
- **Type**: Agent Skill (Claude Code), with a standalone Python evidence extractor
- **Author**: Tatsuya Shimomoto (@shimo4228)
- **License**: MIT
- **Version**: 0.2.0 (2026-08-20; evidence + fresh-context judge redesign) plus unreleased changes in CHANGELOG.md (render evidence, the visible-text / collapsed-floor layout, the visitor read). 0.1.0 (2026-06-08) was the initial lint-based release
- **Language**: Python >= 3.11, run with uv. `readme_evidence.py` uses the standard library only; the optional `readme_render.py` needs Playwright (the one runtime dependency) and an authenticated GitHub CLI
- **Components**: `scripts/readme_evidence.py`, `scripts/readme_render.py`, `references/readme-judge-checklist.md` (+ visual / overview-diagram / ja-register / about / visitor-read / tagline-eval references), `tests/`, `fixtures/`, `evals/`
- **Companion agent**: `readme-judge`, the only agent the skill uses, bundled as `agents/readme-judge.md`; `install.sh` installs the skill and the agent together
- **Status**: active; the skill is synced one way from the author's Claude Code harness (`scripts/sync-from-local.sh`, which never commits), so the harness copy can be ahead between syncs
- **Research line**: component skill of the Authorship Strategy line (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20263316), one of the author's practice lines listed on the hub https://github.com/shimo4228/shimo4228
- **Grounding ADR**: AKC ADR-0008 "Code-LLM Layering" (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19200726)
- **Counterpart skill**: llms-txt-writer (AI surface)

## What is readme-writer?

readme-writer is defined as an Agent Skill that writes and repairs the README: the page a visitor opens first, and the one surface an LLM is guaranteed to ground on when a repo URL is pasted into a chat or surfaced by AI search. Where llms-txt-writer optimizes the AI-only surface (`llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`), this skill owns the human surface. It treats the README as the single canonical human entrance rather than building a separate landing page, because a redundant second page is devalued by AI search and risks fact divergence (cloaking).

## Why does the skill exist?

READMEs grow by accretion: each release adds a bullet, an ADR number, a sibling repository, a coined term. After enough releases a first-time visitor cannot say what the project is for, and an LLM reading only the README cannot reconstruct it. The skill exists to reverse that. Its starting condition is that **the reader must be able to say what the repository is for before any mechanism, install step, or feature list**; if the purpose is not standing, nothing that follows lands. This condition is deliberately not a section template: it may be satisfied by the identity sentence or the lead, and the absence of a "Why this exists" heading is not a defect. The defect is detail starting before purpose.

## What is the "information floor"?

The floor is the small, non-negotiable set of facts an LLM needs to reconstruct the project from the README text alone (not from images or linked files). It lives in a collapsed `<details>` section at the end of the README, which AI assistants that fetch the URL read in full while human visitors skip it: (1) an identity sentence readable in isolation; (2) why the project exists, who it is for, and what distinguishes it; (3) canonical facts such as name, stack, status, and required keys (and whether they are paid), and for research repos the DOI, how-to-cite, and three to six core concept definitions; (4) exactly one concrete example; (5) a pointer-only link map to deeper docs. If the lead promises an artifact ("the history of how the constitution changed"), the README must provide a reachable destination (link, section, or dated count) in the same change. Everything outside the floor is cut or relocated; the floor must not swell into a disguised llms-full.txt.

## How is quality split between code and the LLM?

Following AKC ADR-0008, countable facts are owned by code and contextual judgment by an LLM. `scripts/readme_evidence.py` extracts evidence as JSON: first-screen line count and new-term count, the identity lead, counts of ADR / sibling-repo / docs references, coined-term candidates with occurrence counts, what each `<details>` block contains, the README's size, whether each figure has prose next to it, broken local links and anchors, per-section block layout, badges, slop words and em-dashes, internal-history lines (versions, model swaps), raw numeric claims, and DOI / citation presence. It produces no score, no severity, no threshold, and no failing exit code (exit 0 always; 2 only when the file is missing or oversized). The `readme-judge` agent reads that JSON as one input among several, reads the README once in a fresh context, then checks each claim against the repository's code, and owns the verdict.

## How does the judge decide?

The judge answers a fixed checklist with one line of quoted evidence per question: first screen (R1-R3, R15: identity sentence without unknown terms, tagline, visible text spent on the lead and first-run friction with rationale moved to the collapsed section or docs/, overview-diagram labels matching the text), sentence density (R4-R9: singular reader, active voice, concrete over abstract, one reader-question per paragraph, no slop, no hedging), context budget (R10-R14: coined-term budget of about six with first-use glosses, references as pointers not explanations, internal history only where it answers a question, numbers only where interpretable, Quick Start prerequisites disclosed; R16 names sections to move to docs/ once the raw README passes about 15,000 characters), and six questions generalized from real author findings (K1-K6: as-of consistency, accretion detection, claim logic with a counterexample hunt, unresolved references, missing purpose, promises without destinations). It then runs a refutation pass against its own findings, compares the README against an imagined checklist-perfect version (at least one shortfall must be named even for Publishable), and returns a **named, non-aggregated verdict**: Publishable, Fix (span-level findings only, never a full rewrite), or Rewrite. No numeric score is produced.

## What is the revision loop?

Evidence extraction (and, when available, render evidence), then the judge as a draft gate. For rewrites meant to get people to try a project, three simulated first-time visitors, chosen for the repository, read each draft first and report where they stopped and what pushed them away; wording fixes are made, missing facts go to the author. Publishable moves on; Fix triggers span-level repairs and one recheck with the identical question set; Rewrite stops the loop and returns to the author. The draft loop is capped at two rounds. A binding final judgment with freshly generated questions then runs on the frozen candidate, with a before/after comparison against the pre-rewrite render run twice in swapped order; a Fix there gets span repairs and at most one recheck with the final question set. The judge also checks each claim against the repository's code. The author's read-through is always the top gate, and the number of issues the author finds after the final verdict is recorded as the judge's true error rate.

## Why does the skill produce no quality score?

README quality (human hook, value proposition, narrative) is a semantic judgment with no deterministic base equivalent to the citation research behind AI-surface scorers. A line like `Lead: 6/10` changes nothing; the finding "the lead never says who it is for" changes the next edit. Importing AI-surface metrics (entity density, section ratios) into a human README is an anti-pattern that degrades readability. Word-count targets are likewise rejected as unsourced.

## What does the skill say about figures and visuals?

Prose walls are compressed into scannable structure, not into images. A repository whose mechanism a reader must understand before starting gets one overview diagram (two to four boxes, an SVG per language) right after the lead, with the following paragraph saying the same thing in prose (`references/overview-diagram.md`). In the body, only genuinely graph-shaped content (relations, multi-branch flows) becomes a diagram, preferably Mermaid in top-down orientation; linear three-step processes stay as lists. Every figure carries a one-sentence text equivalent, since text-only extractors and screen readers skip diagrams. Nothing load-bearing lives inside raster images; a collapsed `<details>` section holds only the LLM-read floor at the end, or secondary bulk such as long option tables. Badges are limited to two to four high-signal ones.

## What about Japanese READMEs?

Japanese README body text uses ですます調. The skill records this as a deliberate divergence from the register in the author's article channel contract: a README is a first meeting, and a chain of assertive である sentences reads as intimidating at the entrance. Tables, headings, and noun-ending cells are exempt. Each Japanese paragraph is written on one line, because a line break inside a sentence shows as a space on GitHub. A register table for opening translationese (e.g. 「正本」 into plain phrasing) is in `references/ja-register.md`. Other-language versions keep the same floor, heading hierarchy, anchors, and example, without forcing line-by-line parallelism.

## When should this skill be used, and when not?

Use it to create or improve `README.md` / `README.ja.md`, to repair a README that has grown by accretion, to move long rationale and internal history into `docs/`, or to align the GitHub About (description / topics) with the README's claims. Do not use it for AI-only documents (`llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, FAQ, glossary), which belong to llms-txt-writer; for `graph.jsonld` design (jsonld-knowledge-graph); for cross-surface drift repair (context-sync); or for articles and essays (claude-skill-writing-ecosystem).

## How does it relate to the Authorship Strategy research line?

Authorship Strategy ADR-0006 requires an LLM-facing dual entry point (a prose navigator `llms.txt` plus a concept graph `graph.jsonld`) for every framework-governed artifact. readme-writer covers the third, human-facing surface that those two do not, and keeps its facts consistent with the machine layer so the surfaces do not diverge into cloaking.

## Sibling skills

- llms-txt-writer: the AI-surface counterpart (`llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt`)
- jsonld-knowledge-graph: companion JSON-LD graph for the concept surface
- context-sync: finds overlapping and stale project docs (CLAUDE.md, README, ADRs) and moves each fact to one home
- claude-skill-writing-ecosystem: orchestrator for long-form human prose (articles, essays)
- llm-as-judge: the judge form this skill's verdict follows
